question: A team summarises each of twenty customer interviews, then works only from those summaries to decide which product problems to fix. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The summaries will use the team's own vocabulary rather than the words the interviewed customers actually used.
B) Summarising twenty interviews separately takes longer than reading through all twenty of the transcripts once.
C) The twenty summaries will vary in length, so some interviews will appear to carry more weight than the others do.
D) Details that would identify the real problem are dropped at the summary stage and cannot be recovered later.
correct_answers: D) Details that would identify the real problem are dropped at the summary stage and cannot be recovered later.
explanations: Vocabulary drift is a genuine annoyance and one reason to keep quotes, but it is a milder form of the detail loss described above.
Time spent is a cost of the approach, not a threat to the decision the team is about to make.
Uneven summary lengths are worth normalising, but they signal how much was said rather than distorting what the problems are.

Correct. A summary keeps what seemed important without knowing which decision it will serve. The concrete detail that distinguishes a pricing objection from a trust objection is exactly what gets compressed away, and once the team works only from summaries the loss is invisible.
